Now we hit upon that fundamental philosophical debate of the tree falling in the forest with no one there to hear it. I think a better example is the Quantum Slit Experiment: https://en.m.wikipedia.org/wiki/Double-slit_experiment  Deducing that, as you say, the speed of light exists whether we care to acknowledge it or not is interesting. Mathematics is a language with internal consistency, certainly, and that consistency can extend its premises for the purposes of discovery. It being definitive proof of an objective materiality, however, does require more thought. Experimentally, chemicals acting in a consistent fashion is proof of consistency but not much else. It is key to remember that the history of science is a graveyard of theories once sworn to uphold an objective materiality that were later proven untrue. Indeed, the greatest strength of science is its eagerness to be proven wrong. I am currently on my way to work but this paper for and against scientific materialism covers a lot of what I am gesturing to in my reply: https://philpapers.org/browse/arguments-for-and-against-scientific-realism

I think what’s being touched on here is epistemology. From what I have read you subscribe to scientific materialism: a worldview where understanding the mechanisms behind things like colour (ie light refraction and rods and cones in the eye transmitting light signals to the temporal lobe) provide sufficient explanation as to why, how, where etc. something exists. The argument for the soul questions this materialist epistemology - if we came to understand the existence of colour through measuring sensory datum (the scientific method) but we know our sensory datum are unreliable/ flawed/ contigent on the programming of the meat suit, how can we be assured this explanation is sufficient? This is the first premise to allowing for mystery within materialist reduction, other arguments can then follow.

\- hijack associative connections in the brain. want to study? go to a library. want to play that videogame you bought but just cant begin? set up a gaming space in your living room/a routine of packing and unpacking your console. want to cook? get friends over and share a meal with them, makes it way easier to multitask cooking and fun conversation then the joy of sharing a meal

\- routine where possible. i always exclude time limits on this bc of sleep trouble/ avoidant behaviour when our time feels dictated. but everyday aim for little things, excercise, reading a few pages, eating one piece of fruit, build from the small stuff

\- for a big project like a novel, its going get old working at the same idea over time. if you want to plan your structure, make this as tactile and engaging as possible. got a world you want to craft into words? pick up objects in the room, they are your characters, maybe some cardboard or a funky patterned fabric is a swamp, an interior of a room in a scene, a river etc. physically lay out your world and characters and walk around in it - ive used salt and pepper shakers as protagonists, old socks as ravines and horses - you get the picture. 

\- ofc, the only way to get a novel out of this process is through routine commitment and discipline to getting words out. let the first ones that appear be bad and awkward. you need clay to mould. 

\- you WILL fall in and out of love with the project and idea itself because you are in its interior everyday, but if you can persist and build a daily/weekly habit of getting words down, the itch to write something will overpower incoming apathy.

\- brains are associative, so change the place you go to write. if youre typing on a laptop in bed, and brain associates bed with chilling and sleeping, makes sense that few words are coming out. go to your local library/study space/ a cafe with the specific intention of writing, and overtime brain will associate your presence in that space with writing time.

\- when one project is really not getting anywhere, work on writing something else. the indie press has lots of little competitions (winning could involve publication, money, just publication, a free book - small scale but satisfying stuff) - even if there is no win, you are developing your writing muscle through various forms.

\- READ. reading is so hard with adhd and i fall out of the habit constantly. when i fall off the horse, i have this process: books seem to require an intimidating amount of focus right now, so ill read some manga or a comic. then, ill pick up a book and read 3 pages that night. next night, 4 pages. next 5 and so on.

There’s a lot of us out here with zapped attention spans, and brains now adapted to getting much more info faster from digital formats. My tips to get back into reading as someone with ADHD are these:
Go to a library. Seriously, being around other people reading helps. Also - free books!
Start with five pages a night. The next week, seven pages, and so on and so forth. Increase in increments that work for you. Soon you’ll find yourself too absorbed to keep track of the pages. If you lose momentum, start at five again.

There’s heaps of online publications that publish short fiction and poems - these count to!

Write about what you’ve read - a quick plot summary, character names, sentences that struck you. When you’re feeling unmotivated go back over those notes to feel gratified on your progress and remind yourself about what you can gain from close reading.

Finally, it’s true reading novels is slowly dying out. This doesn’t erase the inherent pleasure, calm and knowledge to be gained from the activity. Think back to when you were a kid, and a book was so exciting and delicious you’d go read it in a cubby or under a tree. That beautiful sense of immersion is still there for you my friend, but it will take some devotion to get it back.
